## Elements

``` bpl
]help •element
```

# `•element` — XML elements

`•element tag` returns an element function for the XML tag `tag`. The
function is displayed as the call that made it, such as
`•element"circle"`. Typing that text makes the same function.

Pass only an attributes record to make an element with no children:
`circle ["r":10]`. Text, a vector of children or an existing element
tree supplies children instead. With both attributes and children, put
the attributes on the left, as in `["x":5] text "Hello"`. An empty right
argument, `""` or
[`⍬`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/zilde.html), gives no
children.

The result is a keyed vector with `tag`, `attrs` and `children` entries.
Notebooks display it as HTML. In that HTML, the text of a `script` or
`style` element isn’t escaped, as browsers require. A `script` element
can hold JavaScript for the page. [XML and SVG](xml.ipynb) covers
element trees.

Errors: `DOMAIN` for invalid tag or attribute names.

Here `span` makes HTML `span` elements. The result is an ordinary keyed
vector. A notebook displays it as HTML, with its `style` attribute
applied:

``` bpl
span←•element "span"
label←["style":"color:steelblue;font-size:1.5em"] span "a < b"
label
```

<span style="color:steelblue;font-size:1.5em">a &lt; b</span>

Given a list of names, `•element` makes one function for each.
`[ul li]←` assigns them to the names `ul` and `li`. Children can be a
vector of elements:

``` bpl
[ul li]←•element "ul" "li"
ul li¨ "ab" "cd"
```

<ul><li>ab</li><li>cd</li></ul>

## XML

``` bpl
]help •xml
```

# `•xml` — XML text

`•xml text` reads XML into an element tree with the same meaning.
Attribute values become text. Names keep their prefixes, and namespace
declarations become `xmlns` attributes. Comments, processing
instructions and text that is only whitespace are dropped. [XML and
SVG](xml.ipynb) covers element trees.

`•xml⁻ tree` writes the XML text of an element tree. It escapes `&`,
[`<`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/less-than.html),
[`>`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/greater-than.html)
and `"` in text and attribute values. An attribute whose value is a
numeric vector is written as space-separated numbers. Children are text,
elements or vectors of children. An element with no children is written
as a self-closing tag.

Errors: `DOMAIN` for malformed XML, and for invalid names or attribute
values given to `•xml⁻`.

`•xml⁻` writes the XML text of an element tree. It escapes `&`,
[`<`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/less-than.html),
[`>`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/greater-than.html)
and `"` in text and attribute values:

``` bpl
•xml⁻ label
```

    "<span style=""color:steelblue;font-size:1.5em"">a &lt; b</span>"

`•xml⁻` writes a numeric vector attribute as space-separated numbers.
Pass an attributes record alone to an element function to make an
element with no children. With two arguments, pass `""` or
[`⍬`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/zilde.html) on the
right to make an element with no children:

``` bpl
polygon←•element "polygon"
•xml⁻polygon ["fill":"red";"points":0 0 10 0 5 8]
```

    "<polygon fill=""red"" points=""0 0 10 0 5 8""/>"

Attribute names keep their case. Prefixed names such as `xlink:href`
pass through unchanged.

## SVG

``` bpl
]help •svg
```

# `•svg` — SVG pictures

`X •svg children` returns an `svg` element with attributes `X`. It adds
`xmlns` for the SVG namespace and `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Attributes in
`X` replace these. With an attributes record as its only argument,
`•svg` returns an empty picture: `•svg ["width":200 "height":100]`. An
argument that is text or an element tree becomes the children unchanged,
as with [`•element`](system/element.qmd). Notebooks display the `svg`
element as a picture. [XML and SVG](xml.ipynb) covers element trees.

`width` and `height` set the picture’s displayed size:

``` bpl
[text circle]←•element "text" "circle"
c←circle ["cx":50 "cy":40 "r":25 "fill":"orange"]
t←["x":50 "y":85 "text-anchor":"middle"] text "Hello"
pic←["width":240 "height":240] •svg c t
pic
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-9-output-1.svg)

Elements are keyed arrays with `tag`, `attrs` and `children` entries.
Edit them using ordinary assignment. Displaying an element serializes
its current tree.

``` bpl
pic.children₀.attrs.fill←"steelblue"
pic
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-10-output-1.svg)

Override `viewBox` with four numbers to choose the drawing coordinates.

``` bpl
["viewBox":0 0 200 100;"width":400;"height":200] •svg pic.children
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-11-output-1.svg)

## Rich display

``` bpl
]help •mime
```

# `•mime` — Rich display

`•mime Y` returns the MIME bundle that display uses for `Y`. The bundle
is a keyed vector from MIME types to text, or to bytes for a binary type
such as `image/png`. It always has `text/plain`. If `Y` has a renderer,
`•mime` calls it with `Y` as
[`ω`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/omega.html) and adds
the entries it returns to the bundle.

The built-in renderers add these types:

- `text/html`: [element functions](system/element.qmd). In the native
  build, a [`•canvas`](system/canvas.qmd) drawing too, as HTML that
  holds its data and the script that draws it.
- `image/svg+xml`: [`•svg`](system/svg.qmd) and
  [`•plot`](system/plot.qmd).
- `image/png`: [`•image`](system/image.qmd). An animation is an animated
  PNG in both builds.
- `image/x-rgba;width=N`: a still `•image` picture in the browser build,
  as RGBA pixels, `N` pixels wide. In JavaScript,
  `new ImageData(new Uint8ClampedArray(bytes.buffer), N)` makes a canvas
  image from the bytes.
- `application/x-bpl-canvas+json` and `application/x-bpl-canvas-data`: a
  `•canvas` drawing in the browser build. The npm package’s `canvas.js`
  is a script whose value is a function that draws it:
  `(0, eval)(script)(canvas, json, bytes)`, where `canvas` is a
  `<canvas>` element and `json` and `bytes` are the two entries.

`F •mime Y` returns `Y` with the renderer that `F` holds, as in
`{["text/html":"</b>",⍨"<b>",⍕ω]}ˢ •mime Y`. With a MIME type as the
left argument, display shows `Y` itself as that type, as in
`"text/markdown" •mime "*hi*"`. An atom becomes a scalar, because only
an array can hold a renderer.

A result keeps a renderer when it has an item for each item of its
argument, as pervasive functions, Each and scans do. Rearranging or
selecting from an array without removing an axis also keeps the
renderer, as reversal, transpose, take, replicate and catenation do.
Changes in place keep the renderer. Other functions drop the renderer,
as reductions and
[`ρ`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/rho.html) do. When
two arguments have different renderers, the result has none. Match
ignores renderers.

Display shows the text form when a renderer fails. Only a direct `•mime`
call reports the error. [Rich display](xml.ipynb#rich-display) covers
renderers.

Errors: `DOMAIN` for a left argument that holds neither a function nor
text.

`F •mime Y` returns `Y` with the renderer that `F` holds. Displaying
that result calls the renderer with `Y` as
[`ω`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/omega.html). The
renderer returns a keyed vector from MIME types to text, or to bytes for
a binary type such as `image/png`. `F` holds the function in an array,
written here with `ˢ`, because a function to the left of `•mime` would
form a train. This renderer shows the sum of `items`:

``` bpl
total←{["text/plain":⍕+/ω.items]}ˢ •mime ["items":[1 2 3]]
total
```

    6

The renderer isn’t one of `total`’s keys. Updating `total` in place
keeps its renderer. The renderer always uses the current values:

``` bpl
total.items+←10
total
```

    36

`•mime total` returns the bundle that display uses for `total`:

``` bpl
•mime total
```

    ["text/plain":"36"]

Pass a MIME type string on the left to display text as that type:

``` bpl
"text/markdown" •mime "**Bold** and *italic*"
```

**Bold** and *italic*

In Python, `basedpl.Array` implements `_repr_mimebundle_()`, which
returns the `•mime` bundle. `bpl(code, 'repl')` returns a `Result` whose
`events` holds the output events in order. `Result.output` lists the
`text/plain` text of each event. `⎕←` produces explicit text output. The
native kernel, notebook magics and `bpl-nb --save` use the whole MIME
bundles.

## Images

``` bpl
]help •image
```

# `•image` — Images

`•image Y` returns a picture: an array of numbers from 0 to 1, with axes
for rows, columns and up to four channels, that notebooks display as an
image. One channel is grey, two are grey and alpha, three are red, green
and blue, and four are red, green, blue and alpha. `Y` is the path of a
PNG or JPEG file, the bytes of one, or the numbers themselves. On a Mac,
`•image` also reads the other formats that macOS’s ImageIO reads, such
as GIF, TIFF, WebP and BMP, with an animation’s frames along a first
axis. On other platforms, `•image` reads PNG and JPEG only. Values
outside 0 to 1 are clipped when the picture is displayed or encoded.

`•image⁻ Y` encodes the picture `Y` as PNG bytes. Its left argument is
an options record with the keys `format` (`"png"` or `"jpeg"`), `fps`
and `delay`. A text left argument gives the format, as in
`"jpeg" •image⁻ Y`. Encoding as JPEG drops the alpha channel.
[`•nput`](system/nput.qmd) writes the bytes to a file, as in
`"out.png" •nput •image⁻ Y`.

An animation has frames along its first axis. A rank-4 array, frames by
rows by columns by channels, is an animation. `["fps":12] •image Y` or
`["delay":0.1] •image Y` treats the first axis of `Y` as frames,
whatever its rank. A grey animation then needs no channel axis. `fps`
sets the frame rate, 24 frames a second by default. `delay` sets the
seconds each frame stays on screen: one number for every frame, or one
per frame. `delay` takes precedence over `fps`.
`["delay":(9ρ0.1),2] •image Y` holds the last of 10 frames for 2
seconds. Notebooks and the [playground](playground.qmd) play an
animation as an animated PNG. `•image⁻` encodes an animation as an
animated PNG, and takes the same options. `•image` reads an animated PNG
back as a rank-4 array, with a channel axis even for grey frames.

Errors: `DOMAIN` for an unknown `format`, invalid image bytes, values
that aren’t real numbers, an `fps` or `delay` that isn’t positive, or an
animation encoded as JPEG; `LENGTH` for a `delay` whose length is
neither 1 nor the number of frames; `RANK` for a shape that isn’t a
picture or an animation; `IO` for file errors.

`•image` displays a matrix of numbers from 0 to 1 as a greyscale
picture. Here each pixel gets brighter with its distance from the
centre:

``` bpl
r←31.5-⍨ι64
pic←•image 1⌊32÷⍨√r²+⊗r²
pic
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-18-output-1.png)

Pervasive functions keep the picture’s renderer. `1-pic` is the
picture’s negative:

``` bpl
1-pic
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-19-output-1.png)

`•image⁻ pic` encodes the picture as PNG bytes. `"out.png" •nput png`
would write those bytes to a file:

``` bpl
png←•image⁻ pic
8↑png
```

    [137 80 78 71 13 10 26 10]ₓ

`•image` also reads PNG and JPEG files. A colour picture has a third
axis, holding each pixel’s red, green and blue:

``` bpl
puppy←•image "puppy.jpg"
ρpuppy
```

    [200 300 3]ₓ

Windows
[`↕`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/up-down-arrow.html)
can shrink it. The second row of `[2 2◇2 2]` gives the movement between
windows, so `[2 2◇2 2]↕puppy` cuts the photo into separate 2×2 blocks of
pixels. Averaging each block halves the picture’s width and height,
making it 150 pixels wide:

``` bpl
small←•image 0.25×+/₂ ₃[2 2◇2 2]↕puppy
small
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-22-output-1.png)

Edge detection needs one brightness value per pixel. An inner product
with the standard luminance weights combines the three colours:

``` bpl
grey←small+.×[0.299 0.587 0.114]
•image grey
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-23-output-1.png)

A Laplacian kernel responds where brightness changes sharply. `3 3↕grey`
gives the 3×3 neighbourhood of every pixel that has one:

``` bpl
k←[0  1 0
   1 ¯4 1
   0  1 0]
win←3 3↕grey
ρwin
```

    [98 148 3 3]ₓ

Multiplying each neighbourhood by the kernel and summing over the last
two axes gives an edge strength for each pixel. Displaying the absolute
values of the edge strengths shows the edges as bright lines:

``` bpl
edges←+/+/k×²win
•image |edges
```

![](xml_files/figure-commonmark/cell-25-output-1.png)
